posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md: Never tried ESPI. But I have done shearography ( [http://www.memagazine.org/backissues/fe ... raphy.html](http://www.memagazine.org/backissues/february99/features/shearography/shearography.html) ) which is very similar. The advantages of shearography pretty much are similar to the advantages of ESPI - low spatial frequency, portability and simplicity of equipment, capture by ccd etc - but the huge advantage of shearography is that it can detect debonding underneath materials - in the z-axis, so to speak. It's become pretty much a standard technique for detection of skin debonding in aircraft. [http://www.ndt.net/article/ecndt02/484/484.htm](http://www.ndt.net/article/ecndt02/484/484.htm)

posts.author: edelbrp
posts.content_md:
> **kc:** BTW edelbrp, do you know how to do the subtraction with photoshop ?

Sure, in a nutshell:

- Open your images in Photoshop

- Drag one image over the other using the tool which looks like a solid black pointer. This will put the image in a new layer in the document.

- Use the arrow keys to 'nudge' the image if nessesary to align it.

- View the layers pallete and select the top layer

- Change the pulldown in the layers pallete from 'Normal' (the default) to 'Difference'. You should immediately see a composite subtracted result between the top layer and the bottom.

You can also continue to move more photos into the same document this way and hide/show different layers by clicking on the eyeball next to the layer in the layers pallete.

Post some more images if you have something interesting to show! 

- Phil

> **kc:** And I just learned from some book and web, they need to view the developed holographic film, under the same laser light got the same wave length that shot the holographic film . Can someone confirm with me about this ? And how am I going to do that on the .jpg file ????

I think this is a different animal. In ESPI, you're recording the speckles (a much more macroscopic point of view). In holograms, you're recording the very small inteference pattern. To 'play back' from the inteference pattern, you need light which has the same wavelength that was used to produce it.[1] Speckles are much coarser and can be recorded by your camera.

BTW-AFAIK, there are no digital mediums that are fine enough to capture inteference patterns in the visible-light spectrum. Even if there were, there would be so much data to store, that it would take a massive harddrive array to record. And, I don't know how it could be reasonably played back... That's why we have to use 'holographic' film, which is really just photographic film with a very high resolving power (like 5000 lines per millimeter!).

-Phil

[1] Well, there are exceptions like when using TEA presoak or postsoak, etc. But, that's a bit off topic.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.content_md:
[quote:d1fd3b4347]And I just learned from some book and web, they need to view the developed holographic film, under the same laser light got the same wave length that shot the holographic film . Can someone confirm with me about this ? And how am I going to do that on the .jpg file ????[/quote:d1fd3b4347]

I think I agree with edelbrp that this is a different animal. I say I think because I'm not familiar with ESPI. However, a few points:

In standard holographic interferometry, you do need to see it in laser light, not necessarily with the same wavelength but it makes life easier if you do use the same wavelength. In this case, you make a laser transmission hologram of the object in the usual way - light reflecting from object and reference light at some angle to the plate - then you distort the object and make another exposure on the same plate. The interference of the two object beams each slightly displaced in phase creates a "beat frequency" which shows up as lines across the image. this is still, however, a laser viewable hologram. The object(s) are still several inches behind the plate and so it (they) cannot be seen in white light without a great deal of dispersion. If you see it in any other than the recording wavelength there will be a magnification of the image and so the apparent beat frequency will be shifted. There may also be other aberrations. This is also true to a lesser extent in shearograms. They're still made with a large enough angle between reference and object to create a high average spatial frequency and the objects are still an inch or so away from the plate. The angle is not as high as a traditional holographic interferometry so you could probably see one with a LED. The fact that you can record the ESPI on ASA 400 film implies to me that this may not be true for ESPI because the spatial frequencies are low enough to be seen in white light without dispersion. I believe ASA 400 corresponds to about 200 l/mm. If you did want to view in laser light, you'd view the negative by transmitting laser light through it.

I was curious why 150 Hz with an exposure of 8 secs. At this rate, there would be 1200 oscillations over an exposure period. I was wondering whether the film would resolve the individual oscillations or would it average over several oscillations? In other words, is the film capture fast enough to capture an event ocurring within with 1/150 sec?

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Do you have your camera set to movie mode with shortest possible exposure? Then record a few seconds of movie. Then use software to separate the individual frames. Take each frame and superimpose it onto the next frame. You may need to put a character on the paper for registration of one frame to the next for superimposition. What I believe happens it the speckle pattern moves at the object is deformed. As you superimpose the frames areas will remain white or begin to get darker from a dark speckle spot depending on the movement direction of the different parts of the object. You may need to superimpose every frame in a sequence or every two or every 5 frames etc... I would imagine, depending on the amout of movement. I would also think the deforming device, in your case a speaker may want to linearly change its frequency from beging to end soas to get a linear movement of the speckle pattern. I would also image that the distance from the object to the camera would also affect the speed at which the speckles move. The further away the slower they would move.

This is purely a thought experiement and not based on practical knowledge. This is a very interesting application, I like it.

I don't think he is recoding fringes per say as that would be impossible with the resolution of a digital camera. I believe he is recording a speckle pattern and moving the speckle pattern with object deformation thus creating smears of light and dark areas. He can probably do the same thing without a reference beam at all going right to the camera. Not sure of the refernce beam thingy as the speckle pattern is caused by the contructive or destructive interference of two or more points coming from the object itself. It may be the reference beam adds light to all interferences causing a greater contrast.

Reference + a completely destructive region gives half reference light

Reference + a completely construtive region gives double reference light

I do agree the the amount of deformation needs to be monitored and modified for the desired effect.

 Posted: Tue Sep 28, 2004 11:48 am Post subject: 

 I must admit I'm very curious about this ESPI. In shearography, it most certainly is a holographic technique, but with a very low average spatial frequency. Low enough, in fact, that it could be captured on "standard film". I

 used holographic film (8E75) but could easily have used PanX. However, the point is that the fringe density is

 in the order of a few hundred lines/mm, but the interference density is low enough to be easily captured by a

 ccd. In fact, that's how shearograms and even holographic interferograms are analysed. But you can't record

 the interference fringes unless you can first record the holographic fringes. In other words, you need high

 (-ish) film resolution to capture the data but can analyse the data at a very much lower resolution. You can see

 that from the following equations: 

[http://images.techonline.com/images/com ... ation1.gif](http://images.techonline.com/images/community/content/old/features/OSEE/B80/equation1.gif) 

[http://images.techonline.com/images/com ... ation2.gif](http://images.techonline.com/images/community/content/old/features/OSEE/B80/equation2.gif) 

 from the tutorial site: [http://www.techonline.com/community/ed_ ... icle/14420](http://www.techonline.com/community/ed_resource/feature_article/14420) 

 The digital medium need only capture delta (theta) not theta itself. The interesting thing is the disappearance of the sin squared term in equation two and the factor of 4. Equation 2 is a standard two beam interference while eqn 1 is a very rapid oscillation with a much slower envelope and twice the amplitude. But there's no indication of the other which contributes to delta theta in delta theta. What is being subtracted? Or is delta theta just a random translation of theta itself? 

 The other intriguing thing is that speckle is very much tied to the resolution of the capture device (the pupil of

 the eye, in terms of vision). In the case of ESPI, is the speckle size itself tied to the grain size, and hence the

 resolution, of the film? In which case, wouldn't delta theta be very dependant on the grain size?
